builder_plan.scenario: Your inference service slows down when several customers send requests together.
builder_plan.change: Replay a recorded request trace with only the proposed serving policy changed.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current scheduler on the same model and hardware.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Requests meeting your latency target, throughput, failures, and cost per successful request.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
summary: Flide replaces generation-oriented serving stacks (vLLM/SGLang) that recompute shared prefixes or distort probabilities when executing branching decision-model queries, instead flattening the logical request tree into one token stream with GPU-resident fork metadata and checkpointed agent histories. It requires adopting a custom inference engine with ForkAttention over both standard attention and Gated DeltaNet layers, plus pre-recorded execution graphs, which adds integration and maintenance cost beyond commodity serving frameworks. It can fail if the workload is not dominated by branching categorical decision queries, if the specific decision/hybrid models (e.g., Jev-style or Gated DeltaNet architectures) are not the ones deployed, or if the unreleased/immature implementation cannot be operated on a single 24 GB GPU within a small team's budget.
rationale: The 9.5x claim targets a specialized decision-inference pattern with custom kernels and engine adoption, so it is worth tracking but premature to adopt before the software, model compatibility, and workload fit are independently verified.
technique: Exact state forking for decision-model inference

claims.statement: Flide replaces generation-oriented serving stacks (vLLM/SGLang) that recompute shared prefixes or distort probabilities when executing branching decision-model queries, instead flattening the logical request tree into one token stream with GPU-resident fork metadata and checkpointed agent histories. It requires adopting a custom inference engine with ForkAttention over both standard attention and Gated DeltaNet layers, plus pre-recorded execution graphs, which adds integration and maintenance cost beyond commodity serving frameworks. It can fail if the workload is not dominated by branching categorical decision queries, if the specific decision/hybrid models (e.g., Jev-style or Gated DeltaNet architectures) are not the ones deployed, or if the unreleased/immature implementation cannot be operated on a single 24 GB GPU within a small team's budget.
Answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance.
